Considered by many scientists the fastest fish in the ocean,[8] sailfish were previously estimated to reach maximum swimming speeds of 35 m/s (125 km/h; 80 mph), but research published in 2015 and 2016 indicate sailfish do not exceed speeds between 10–15 m/s (35–55 km/h; 20–35 mph).
During predator–prey interactions, sailfish reached burst speeds of 7 m/s (25 km/h; 15 mph) and did not surpass 10 m/s (35 km/h; 20 mph).[9][10]
As a result, the sailfish usually attacks sardine schools from behind, putting at risk those fish that are the rear of the school because of their reduced swimming speeds.[20]
1 2 Marras S, Noda T, Steffensen JF, Svendsen MBS, Krause J, Wilson ADM, Kurvers RHJM, Herbert-Read J & Domenic P 2015) "Not so fast: swimming behavior of sailfish during predator–prey interactions using high-speed video and accelerometry".
↑ Svendsen MBS, Domenici P, Marras S, Krause J, Boswell KM, Rodriguez-Pinto I, Wilson ADM, Kurvers RHJM, Viblanc PE, Finger JS & Steffensen JF (2016) "Maximum swimming speeds of sailfish and other large marine predatory fish species based on muscle contraction time: A myth revisited".
Sailfish grow quickly, reaching 1.2–1.5 m (4–5 ft) in length in a single year, and feed on the surface or at middle depths on smaller pelagic forage fish and squid.
Generally, sailfish do not grow to more than 3 m (10 ft) in length and rarely weigh over 90 kilograms (200 pounds).
Sailfish live in colder pelagic waters of all Earth's oceans, and hold the record for the highest speed of any marine animal.
The injuries that sailfish inflict on their prey appear to reduce their swimming speeds, with injured fish being more frequently found in the back (compared with the front) of the school than uninjured ones.

The cheetah is a pursuit predator and the fastest land animal, capable of running at 93–104 km/h (58–65 mph); it has evolved for speed, having powerful hindlimb muscles and a long lumbar spine.
The cheetah is the fastest land animal, capable of overtaking pronghorns and fast antelopes, even when they have a 137 m (449 ft) head start.[82][89] Cheetahs can easily outrun greyhounds in a race.[90] A popular figure of 114 km/h (71 mph) has been discredited due to a faulty measurement method.[82] The highest reliably reported running speed is 104 km/h (65 mph).[91][72] A speed of 100.1 km/h (62.2 mph) also has been reliably reported.[92] An 11 year old cheetah from the Cincinnati Zoo was measured at a speed of 98 km/h (61 mph).[93]
Cheetahs equipped with GPS collars hunted at speeds lower than the highest speeds attained; the average running speed recorded during hunts was 54 km/h (34 mph), while the highest speed recorded was 93 km/h (58 mph).[94] The cheetah uses its maximum running speed only to close the distance with the prey in a straight line, then it follows closely during 3–4 twists in zigzag that the prey makes trying to escape.[61] The speeds of more than 100 km/h (62 mph) attained by the cheetah are greater than those achieved typically by the pronghorn and fast antelopes at 80 km/h (50 mph).[82][89] But the cheetah has an exceptional acceleration, from 0 to 97 km/h (0 to 60 mph) in less than 3 seconds.[75][95] For comparison, polo horses can go from 0 to 36 km/h (0 to 22 mph) in 3.6 seconds.[96]

A typical, unhurried soaring speed in golden eagles is around 45–52 kilometres per hour (28–32 mph).[51] When hunting or displaying, the golden eagle can glide very fast, reaching speeds of up to 190 kilometres per hour (120 mph).[4][50] When stooping (diving) in the direction of prey or during territorial displays, the eagle holds its legs up against its tail, and holds its wings tight and partially closed against its body.
When diving after prey, a golden eagle can reach 240 to 320 kilometres per hour (150 to 200 mph).[52][53] Although less agile and manoeuvrable, the golden eagle is apparently quite the equal and possibly even the superior of the peregrine falcon's stooping and gliding speeds.[5][54] This makes the golden eagle one of the two fastest living animals.[22] Although most flight in golden eagles has a clear purpose (e.g., territoriality, hunting), some flights, such as those by solitary birds or between well-established breeding pairs, seem to be play.[5][17][55]
Golden eagles use their agility and speed combined with powerful feet and large, sharp talons to hunt a variety of prey, mainly hares, rabbits, marmots, and other ground squirrels.[4]
↑ Darling, F.F. (1934). "Speed of a Golden Eagle's flight".
Weight is from 2.9 to 6 kg (6.4 to 13.2 lb) with no known reports of average masses.[4][15] This subspecies is slightly smaller and darker plumaged than the nominate subspecies, but it is not as dark as the golden eagles found further to the east.
The golden eagle is a very large raptor, 66 to 102 centimetres (26 to 40 in) in length.
The only species in the genus Aquila that exceeds the golden eagle in average wingspan and length is the wedge-tailed eagle of Australasia; however, the wedge-tailed eagle is a slightly less heavy bird.[22]

A study testing the flight physics of an "ideal falcon" found a theoretical speed limit at 400 km/h (250 mph) for low-altitude flight and 625 km/h (388 mph) for high-altitude flight.[59] Some sources state that the peregrine falcon can reach over 320 km/h (200 mph) during its stoop,[19] which would make it the fastest animal on the planet.[60][61][62] According to a National Geographic TV program, in 2005 Ken Franklin recorded a falcon stooping at a top speed of 389 km/h (242 mph).[63][64] Other sources state that radar tracks have never confirmed these kinds of speeds, with the highest reliably measured being 184 km/h (114 mph).[65]
In addition, peregrines have been documented preying on chicks in nests, from birds such as kittiwakes.[84] Prey is plucked before consumption.[52] A 2016 study showed that the presence of peregrines benefits non-preferred species while at the same time causing a decline in its preferred prey.[85] As of 2018, the fastest recorded falcon was at 242 mph (nearly 390 km/h).
A video of the falcon stooping at a top speed of 389 km/h (242 mph).
Peregrine falcons have a flicker fusion frequency of 129 Hz (cycles per second), very fast for a bird of its size, and much faster than mammals.[53]
↑ McMillan, Fiona (13 April 2018). "Falcon Attack: How Peregrine Falcons Maneuver At Nearly 225 MPH".
The peregrine falcon (Falco peregrinus), sometimes referred to simply as the peregrine,[3] is a bird of prey (raptor) in the family Falconidae known for its speed.

The Chiron's top speed is electronically limited to 420 km/h (261 mph), or 375–380 km/h (233–236 mph) without the specific key, for safety reasons, mainly arising from the tyres as Bugatti concluded that no tyre currently manufactured would be able to handle the stress at the top speed the Chiron is capable of achieving.[21][22] Independent testing by an owner has indicated that the Chiron can easily attain its limited top speed.[23] Mixed fuel consumption is 22.5 L/100 km (12.55 mpg‑imp; 10.45 mpg‑US).[24]
At the 2017 IAA show in Frankfurt, Bugatti announced that the Chiron broke the record of fastest 0–400–0 km/h (0–249–0 mph) acceleration time, completing it in 41.96 seconds in a span of 3.2 kilometres (2 miles) at the Ehra-Lessien high-speed oval on a weekend in August 2017.[68] The car was driven by Colombian racing driver Juan Pablo Montoya.[69][70][71]
On 2 August 2019, Bugatti test driver Andy Wallace achieved a speed of 490.484 km/h (304.773 mph) in a pre-production Chiron Super Sport 300+ prototype at Volkswagen's test facility in Ehra-Lessien.
↑ Perkins, Chris (2012-06-21). "The Bugatti Chiron Can't Max Out its 310-MPH Speedo Until Someone Makes a Tire That Can Withstand Those Speeds".
↑ "Bugatti Chiron Hits 261 MPH in New Top Speed Run, Sounds Like a Jet Fighter Blasting Off".
↑ Sluys, Andrew (2019-09-03). "Watch: Bugatti Chiron hits 490km/h in a record-breaking speed run".
Without the limiter, Bugatti claimed the car could attain a maximum speed in excess of 483 km/h (300 mph), with 490 km/h (304.7 mph) being achieved in August 2019 with a pre-production model.
In its final production form, the Chiron SS 300+ has different seats, no roll-cage, standard ride height and an electronically limited top speed of 440 km/h (273.4 mph).[73][74]

The Tōkaidō Shinkansen began service on 1 October 1964, shortly before the opening of the 1964 Tokyo Olympics on 10 October 1964.[28] Prior to the introduction of the high-speed line, conventional limited express services required approximately 6 hours and 40 minutes to travel between Tokyo and Osaka.[citation needed] With the opening of the Shinkansen, the limited-stop Hikari service reduced the journey time to four hours, while the all-stations Kodama service completed the trip in five hours.[29] The first Shinkansen trains, the 0 series, ran at speeds of up to 210 km/h (130 mph), later increased to 220 km/h (137 mph), reducing end-to-end trip times on Hikari services to three hours and ten minutes.[citation needed]
Since 2014, Shinkansen trains run regularly at speeds up to 320 km/h (200 mph) on the Tōhoku Shinkansen; only the Shanghai maglev train, China Railway High-speed networks, and the Indonesian Jakarta-Bandung High-speed railway have commercial services that operate faster.[35][36][needs update]
While operating on the mini-Shinkansen lines trains have a maximum speed of 130 kilometres per hour (81 mph).
In 2025, JR West introduced shortened N700A series trains from 16 to 8 cars to replace the 500 series on the San'yō Shinkansen Kodama service with a maximum operating speed of 285 km/h (177 mph).
800 series – 6-car trainsets introduced in March 2004 on the Kyushu Shinkansen with a maximum speed of 260 km/h (160 mph).
N700-7000/8000 series – 8-car trainsets introduced in March 2011 on the Kyushu Shinkansen with a maximum speed of 300 km/h (185 mph).
N700S-8000 series – 6-car trainsets introduced in 2022 on the Nishi Kyushu Shinkansen with a maximum speed of 260 km/h (160 mph).[63]

Similar to the July 2024 failure, this anomaly was also caused by a liquid oxygen leak in the upper stage's engine.[130] In March 2025, a Falcon 9 booster was lost when it caught fire and tipped over after a droneship landing following a Starlink launch.[122] This failure was blamed on a fuel leak that occurred inside one of the first stage engines during ascent.[131] Space journalist Eric Berger has argued that the main factor behind the recent anomalies is SpaceX's "ever-present pressure to accelerate, even while taking on more and more challenging tasks", noting that the company may have reached "the speed limit for commercial spaceflight".
Additionally, the fairing halves are scooped out of water after a parachute-assisted landing and can be reflown multiple times.[19] As of November 12, 2026, SpaceX has successfully landed Falcon 9 boosters 660 times.[e] Individual boosters have flown as many as 37 flights.[20] Both stages are powered by SpaceX Merlin engines,[f] using cryogenic liquid oxygen and rocket-grade kerosene (RP-1) as propellants.[21][22]
SpaceX originally intended to follow its Falcon 1 launch vehicle with an intermediate capacity vehicle, Falcon 5.[41] The Falcon line of vehicles are named after the Millennium Falcon, a fictional starship from the Star Wars film series.[42] In 2005, SpaceX announced that it was instead proceeding with Falcon 9, a "fully reusable heavy-lift launch vehicle", and had already secured a government customer.

On 14 November 1994, Eurostar services began running from Waterloo International station in London, to Paris Nord, as well as to Brussels-South railway station.[8][15][16] The train service started with a limited Discovery service; the full daily service started on 28 May 1995,[17] with a typical Waterloo-Paris Nord trip taking 2 hours and 55 minutes,[18] with an average end-to-end speed of 171.5 km/h (106.6 mph) from London to Paris.[19]
On 30 July 2003, a Eurostar train set a new British speed record of 334.7 km/h (210 mph) on the first section of the "High Speed 1" railway between the Channel Tunnel,[12][15] and Fawkham Junction in north Kent, two months before official public services began running.
On 7 October 2010, it was reported that Eurostar had selected Siemens as preferred bidder to supply 10 Siemens Velaro[310] train sets at a cost of €600 million[311] These would be sixteen-car, self-propelled, 400 m-long (1,300 ft) train sets built to meet Channel Tunnel requirements.[312] The top speed of the e320 train sets is 320 km/h (200 mph) with 902 seats, compared to the e300 fleet which has a top speed of 300 km/h (186 mph) and a seating capacity of 750.
On 5 June 2000, a Eurostar train travelling from Paris to London derailed on the LGV Nord high-speed line while travelling at 290 km/h (180 mph).
The trains are essentially modified TGV sets,[296][297] and can operate at up to 300 km/h (185 mph) on high-speed lines, and 160 km/h (100 mph) in the Channel Tunnel.[69] It is possible to exceed the 300 km/h speed limit, but only with special permission from the safety authorities in the respective country.[298] Speed limits in the Channel Tunnel are dictated by air-resistance, energy (heat) dissipation and the need to be used with other, slower trains.
